Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

vignette: Dale Santos, a fifty-year-old American of South Eastern Asian descent, had spent the last six months carefully narrowing his world to the familiar. It began with a series of escalating encounters that slowly rewired how he moved through his own city. A listener from an early coffeehouse set, who had first complimented his guitar work and later appeared at his apartment lobby, eventually slipped a folded note under his door detailing his exact rehearsal hours. The next evening, Dale found his amplifiers rearranged in the practice room, a specific chord chart he had never used placed on the stool, and the faint scent of damp wool lingering near the exits. He tried to reconstruct the lead-up, to trace how the person had first learned his routines, but the memory simply refused to cohere. Where there should have been a sequence of calls, meetings, or sightings, there was only a hard, absolute blank. When pieces of the experience did surface, they arrived without warning, vivid and total. A sudden flash of a leather collar, the exact scrape of a chair leg against hardwood, the taste of metallic fear in his throat would flood him all at once, then dissolve as quickly as they came, leaving him staring at his hands, waiting for the next fragment. He had come to believe that the precinct officers and the label’s security desk had let him down, that the people and systems meant to shield him were fundamentally ill-equipped to stop someone who simply refused to leave. Over the following months, his habits solidified. He stopped accepting booking requests for venues in unfamiliar neighborhoods because he told himself he could not assess the danger in spaces where he did not know the sightlines or the back doors. Instead, he drove the same route to the only downtown rehearsal studio that had been his for years. There, he would pause at the threshold, watching other musicians who arrived early, checking their shoulders for sudden turns, noting the angle of their hands, listening to the rhythm of their footsteps. What frightened him most was the ordinary. A patron lingering near the back row, a driver idling too long outside the loading dock, a glance held a beat too long across the room. He would scan the balconies and side corridors until the band arrived, mapping every possible approach before he touched a string. At night, the difference between day and night felt like a shift in gravity. During daylight, the streets were populated, the rhythm of daily life offered a kind of buffer. After dusk, his apartment felt hollow and exposed. He kept the overhead lights burning, slept in his work clothes, and found it harder to feel safe the moment the streetlights clicked on. The music he had once played with instinctive joy now felt distant, muffled by a thick, internal quiet. He was certain he was a weak person for not having anticipated the escalation, for not having changed his locks sooner, for letting it persist so long. He told himself that a stronger man would have shut the door completely, that his inability to control the situation proved his own fragility. The routine of avoidance had quietly rewritten his professional life. He declined a residency at a new arts center because the application required a walk-through of a wing he had never visited. His divorce, which had begun with quiet frustrations over his unreliability and emotional distance, had long since settled into a quiet, final separation. The studio owner stopped asking him to cover extra shifts. The gigs he did take were limited to venues he had played before, and even then, he arrived twenty minutes early to chart the room, scanning the crowd until his shoulders ached. He kept doing it because the alternative felt impossible. What brought him to the clinic last Tuesday was not a single breakdown, but the cumulative weight of waking up before dawn, driving the familiar route to the same studio, and realizing he no longer recognized the man in the mirror. He did not want to be a prisoner of his own routines, nor did he want the music to disappear entirely. He was hoping, quietly, for a way to step outside his own perimeter without feeling like he was walking into a trap.
